title: Threat Modeling for Enterprise Secure Messaging Applications
venue: Unpublished / preprint (no journal or conference venue stated in the document)
one_line: A conceptual study that applies structured threat-modeling frameworks (STRIDE, PASTA, Attack Trees, MITRE ATT&CK) to enterprise secure messaging apps and proposes a tailored threat-modeling process with technical, administrative, and monitoring mitigations.
problem: Many enterprise messaging platforms lack systematic threat modeling, leaving them exposed to data leakage, unauthorized access, phishing/impersonation, and insider threats. There is limited research focused specifically on enterprise messaging applications and on integrating threat modeling with continuous security testing.
methods: Mixed-method (qualitative threat identification plus quantitative likelihood/impact scoring). Proposes a six-step threat-modeling process: asset identification, attack-surface analysis, threat enumeration (STRIDE/PASTA), vulnerability assessment, risk analysis (likelihood/impact risk matrix), and mitigation strategies. Tools cited include Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool and OWASP Threat Dragon, plus penetration-testing frameworks and security logging/anomaly-detection systems. Validation via case studies of popular platforms and controlled attack simulations.
key_findings: Threats to enterprise messaging were categorized via STRIDE: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, and elevation of privilege.
High-priority threats were frequently associated with human factors (insider misuse) and integration points such as APIs and third-party services.
Case studies revealed recurring vulnerability patterns: insufficient access-control enforcement and incomplete encryption coverage.

Mitigations are grouped into technical controls (E2EE, multi-factor authentication, hardened APIs, secure endpoints), administrative controls (policies, awareness training, incident response), and continuous monitoring (logging, anomaly detection, alerting).
Future work suggests integrating AI-driven anomaly detection with threat modeling and embedding automated threat modeling in DevSecOps pipelines.
strengths: Provides a clear, messaging-specific threat-modeling workflow grounded in established frameworks (STRIDE, PASTA, MITRE ATT&CK).
Organizes mitigations into a practical technical/administrative/monitoring taxonomy useful for design-stage projects.
Explicitly identifies insider threats and API integration points as high-priority risk areas, aligning with real enterprise concerns.
weaknesses: No quantitative experimental results, datasets, or measured metrics are reported; risk scoring is described conceptually only.
Validation relies on simulations and case studies that the author notes may not replicate real operational environments, limiting generalizability.
Document lacks a formal published venue and is light on technical depth for cryptographic or authentication countermeasures.
relevance: This paper supplies the threat-model backbone for SentriZK's Domain 1 motivation: it enumerates the exact attack vectors SentriZK targets (unauthorized access/spoofing, data interception, insider threats) and frames mitigations as E2EE, strong authentication, and anomaly/insider-threat monitoring. Its future-work call to fuse AI-driven anomaly detection with threat modeling directly motivates SentriZK's on-device AI threat-detection pillar, while its emphasis on authentication and human-factor risks supports the case for zero-knowledge-proof authentication.
ieee_reference: M. Ilesanmi, "Threat modeling for enterprise secure messaging applications," 2025. (unpublished)
